column2: All of those, the supreme scripture says, become purified of sin; one slain in battle for a Brahmana's sake is freed from the sin of Brahmin-slaying.
A slayer of a Brahmana who gives a hundred thousand cows to worthy recipients is freed from all sins.
One who gives twenty-five thousand tawny milch cows is freed from all sins.
One who gives a hundred Kamboja horses to restrained Brahmanas, lord of the earth, is freed from the sin.
One who fulfils a wish of even one person, Bharata, and does not proclaim it after giving, is freed from sin.
A twice-born who once drinks wine, and then drinks it fire-hot, purifies himself here and hereafter.
By falling from Mount Meru, or entering fire, or undertaking the great departure, one is freed of all sins.
A Brahmana who has drunk wine, having sacrificed with the Brihaspati-sava, should go again to the assembly of Brahmanas—so says the Brahmana scripture.
One who, free of envy, gives a gift of land after drinking wine and does not drink again, O king, being purified is cleansed.
One who defiles his teacher's bed should lie on a heated iron slab, or with his organ in his hand go forth looking upward.
By leaving the body he is freed from the evil deed; women are freed from their deeds by restraint for a year.
One who practises the great vow and gives all his wealth, or is slain in battle for his teacher, is freed from the evil deed.
One who has served by falsehood or obstructed his teacher, having brought him something pleasing, is freed from that sin.
For breaking the vow of celibacy, one should practise the vow for Brahmin-slaying, wearing an ass's hide for six months; thus he is freed from the offence.
An abductor of another's wife and one taking another's property, keeping the vow for a year, is likewise freed from the offence.
One from whom something is stolen should be given equal wealth; by various means he is freed from the offence.
By hardship for twelve days, well practised, or at least ten, the younger brother married before the elder and the elder unmarried become pure, Bharata.
The marriage of the younger should be arranged by him, who ever saves his ancestors; there is no fault in the woman, and she is not stained by it.
In union the woman is pure by her season; the Chaturmasya rite is prescribed; women are thereby purified, so those who know dharma say.
Women suspected of sin are not to be approached by one who knows; they are purified by their menses as a vessel by ashes.
Dharma is fourfold and complete for Brahmanas; for the kshatriya a quarter less, so dharma is ordained.
Likewise for the Vaishya and Shudra a quarter each is ordained; by such a rule know the weightiness and lightness of their duties.
Having slain animals, and cut many other trees, a man should live three nights on air and make his deed known.
For intercourse with the forbidden, O king, expiation is prescribed: wearing wet clothes for six months, he should live lying in ashes.
This same rule would apply to all the things not to be done, by the rule declared by Brahmanas, with examples, scriptures and reasons.
One who recites the Savitri in a pure place, with moderate food, harmless, unhurried and silent, is freed from all offences.
He should stay in the open air by day and sleep under the sky at night; three times by day and three times by night, he should enter water with his clothes on.
In the vow he should not speak to women, Shudras or outcasts; having done sins unknowingly, the twice-born is freed by this vow.
After death one receives the fruit of good and evil, with beings as witnesses; whichever of the two is greater, that fruit the doer receives.
Therefore by giving, austerity and action one should increase the good fruit after doing evil, so as to have the excess.
One should do good deeds in the matter of sinful deeds and give wealth always; thus he is freed from the offence.
Expiation is declared corresponding to the sin; expiation is prescribed excepting the great sins.
In all matters of the edible and the forbidden, the speakable and unspeakable, O king, those who know allow distinctions between ignorance and knowledge.
A sin done knowingly becomes wholly heavy; for a fault in a lapse from ignorance, expiation is prescribed.
Sin can be removed by the rule as stated; this rule is prescribed for the believing and faithful.
This rule is never seen for unbelievers and faithless men, in whom the fault of hypocrisy predominates.
The conduct of the good and the good one, best of those who uphold dharma, tiger among men, are to be followed by one who wishes happiness here and hereafter.
You, O king, will be freed from sin by that former reason, whether in saving or in slaying them, or by action.
Or if you feel any disgust, you will perform expiation; but do not meet death by a deed practised by the ignoble."
What is edible and what forbidden, what is to be given and praised, and who is a worthy and who an unworthy recipient—tell me that, grandsire.
[Vyasa said:] "Here they recite this ancient history, the dialogue of the perfected with Manu, the Prajapati.
Long ago the perfected, devoted to austerity and vows, gathered and asked about dharma the lord seated, the Prajapati of the beginning:
'How is food, how is giving, how is study, how is austerity, and what is to be done and not done? Tell us all that, Prajapati.'
Thus addressed, the revered Manu Svayambhuva said: 'Listen to dharma briefly, Vyasa, as it is.
Not taking what is not given, giving, study, austerity, non-violence, truth, freedom from anger, forbearance and sacrifice are the marks of dharma.
That which is dharma becomes adharma in the wrong place and time; taking, falsehood and violence are held to be dharma by circumstance.
For those who know dharma and adharma, both are twofold: inaction and action—the twofold in the world and in the Veda.
Ten who know the Veda and scriptures, or three who recite dharma, what they say when a matter arises is dharma, in a doubt about dharma.
Red earth, ants, the shleshmataka fruit, and poison are forbidden to Brahmanas.
Fish without scales are forbidden to Brahmanas; of quadrupeds, other than the tortoise; frogs and water-creatures;
bhasa birds, swans, Garuda-like birds, chakravakas, cranes, plavas, herons, madgu birds, vultures, kalolukas;
all flesh-eating birds and tusked quadrupeds, those with teeth in both jaws and those with four tusks.
A Brahmana should not drink the milk of ewes, mares, she-asses, camels, cows that have just calved, women and deer.
Food of the dead and of the newly delivered, anything unprepared, and milk of a cow before ten days, is not to be eaten or drunk.
Food of a carpenter, a leather-cutter, an unchaste woman, a washerman, a physician, and a guard is not to be eaten.
Nor of those cursed by guilds or villages, those who live on the stage or on women, the married-before-elder, eunuchs, bards and gamblers.
Food brought when refused, sour, stale, accompanied by liquor, left over and remnants are not to be eaten.
Preparations of flour, meat, sugarcane and vegetables, and milk, barley meal, parched grain and gruel kept long are not to be eaten.
Payasa, krisara, meat and cakes made for no purpose are not to be eaten by householder Brahmanas.
Having worshipped gods, ancestors, men, sages and the household deities, the householder may then eat.
As a mendicant who has gone forth lives, so a householder in his own house; living thus with dear wives he obtains dharma.
A righteous man should not give a gift for fame, nor from fear, nor to a benefactor, nor to those who dance, sing or jest.
Nor to the drunk or mad, nor to a thief or physician, nor to the speechless, discoloured, limb-deficient or dwarf.
Nor to a wicked man or one of bad family, or one not refined by vows; a gift to an unlearned Brahmana who does not expound Brahma is dead.
What is given improperly and accepted improperly leads to harm for both, giver and taker.
As one who clings to a khadira branch or a stone and crosses the sea sinks, so sink the giver and the receiver.
As fire spread with wet wood does not blaze, so the recipient lacking austerity, Vedic study and character.
As water in a skull or milk in a dog's skin, so learning in one lacking conduct, through the fault of the vessel.
One who is without mantras, vows, scripture and free of envy, to him out of compassion one should give, even among the wretched.
Out of compassion one should not give even to a wretched wrongdoer; "It is the practice of the trustworthy" or "It is dharma"—that is the reason.
What is given to a Brahmana devoid of dharma is without cause, it is from the fault of an unworthy recipient; I have no doubt here.
As a wooden elephant, as a leather deer, so is a Brahmana who has not studied; the three bear only the name.
As a eunuch is fruitless among women, as a cow is fruitless with a cow, as a bird is wingless, so is a Brahmana without mantras.
As a village's grain is empty, as a well is waterless, as an oblation is in a fireless place, so is one rejected.
A fool who is a destroyer of the oblations for gods and ancestors, an enemy, a robber of wealth, cannot attain the worlds.'
All this has been told to you as it was, Yudhishthira, briefly; this great matter is to be heard, bull of the Bharatas."

If you wish to hear dharma in full, Yudhishthira, go to Bhishma, mighty-armed, the old grandsire of the Kurus.

Thus addressed, the son of Kunti, of long insight and great splendour, said to Vyasa, son of Satyavati, best of speakers:

Having made a very great, hair-raising slaughter of kinsmen, the doer of a wrong to the whole world, destroyer of the earth,
mahabharata:12:38.19	having had him slain in the battle by trickery, that straight fighter, for what reason should I dare to approach him?
Then the mighty-armed, greatly radiant best of the Yadus again said to that best of kings, wishing the good of the four classes:

Now you ought not to persist too strongly in grief; do what the revered Vyasa says, best of kings.
mahabharata:12:38.22	The Brahmanas and your mighty brothers wait on you, mighty-armed one, hoping like the sun-tormented for the rain-god.
mahabharata:12:38.23	The remaining kings are slain and the whole four-class realm has come together, great king, your Kurujangala kingdom.
mahabharata:12:38.24	For the pleasure of these great-souled Brahmanas and at the command of the teacher Vyasa of immeasurable splendour,

Thus addressed by Krishna, the lotus-eyed king, the great ascetic, rose for the welfare of all the world.
Persuaded by Vistarashravas himself, tiger among men, and by Dvaipayana, and by Devasthana and Jishnu,
persuaded by these and many others, the high-minded Yudhishthira cast off mental sorrow and anguish.
Learned in what is heard, a treasure of the heard, skilled in all that is to be heard, the delight of Pandu resolved and attained peace of mind.
Surrounded by them like the moon by stars, the king entered his own city, putting Dhritarashtra before him.
Wishing to enter, the righteous son of Kunti, Yudhishthira, honoured the gods and thousands of Brahmanas.
Then he mounted a new, bright chariot covered with blankets and deerskins, yoked with sixteen white, auspicious-marked oxen,
honoured with holy mantras and praised by great sages, as the god Soma his nectar-made chariot.
The son of Kunti, Bhima of terrible valour, took the reins; Arjuna held the white umbrella, sun-bright.
That white umbrella held over his head shone like the moon among the stars, like cloud in the sky.
The two heroes, sons of Madri, adorned, held the white chowries, radiant like moonbeams.
Those five brothers, mounted on the chariot, adorned, appeared then like all the elements, O king.
Mounting a bright chariot yoked with swift horses, Yuyutsu followed behind, O king, the elder of the Pandavas.
Krishna, with Satyaki, mounted a bright golden chariot yoked with Sainya and Sugriva and followed the Kurus.
The eldest (Dhritarashtra), borne by men, went with Gandhari in front of Partha's father (Dharmaraja).
And all the Kuru women, Kunti, Krishna Draupadi, went in vehicles high and low, led by Vidura.
Then many chariots and adorned elephants, foot-soldiers and horses followed behind.
Then praised by bards, charioteers and Magadhas with fine words, the king went to the city of Nagasahvaya (Hastinapura).
That procession of the mighty-armed one was incomparable on earth, crowded, overflowing, filled with glad and well-fed people.
For Partha's entry, the people of the city had duly adorned the city and the royal road.
The royal road was covered with white garlands, banners and platforms, and well perfumed with incense.
With powders of fragrance and various flowers and priyangu, and with garlands hung, the royal palace was surrounded.
At the city gate were set firm new jars filled with water, maidens, flowers and goats here and there.
Thus the son of Pandu, praised with auspicious words, surrounded by friends, entered the city with its gates adorned.
That royal road, with its crossings adorned, shone, O king, like the swelling ocean at moonrise.
The houses on the royal road, large and full of jewels, seemed to tremble under the weight of the women who filled them.
Those women, as if shyly, softly praised Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Arjuna and the two Pandavas, sons of Madri.

You are fortunate, Panchali, who wait on the best of men, auspicious one, as Gautami on great sages.
mahabharata:12:39.6	Your deeds are not in vain, and your vow-keeping, lady. Thus the women praised Krishna, great king.
With their words of praise and mutual sounds and sounds born of joy, the city was filled.
Passing along the royal road, Yudhishthira reached the royal palace, adorned and shining.
Then all the people, townsfolk and country folk, came up and spoke ear-pleasing words here and there.
Be our king here, great king, for a hundred autumns; protect the subjects by dharma as Indra does heaven.
Thus at the gate of the royal house, honoured with auspicious things and receiving blessings spoken by the twice-born on all sides,
the king entered the palace like the house of the king of the gods, and, hearing words joined to victory, descended afterward from the chariot.
Entering within, the glorious one went to the deities and worshipped them with jewels, perfumes and garlands.
Then the glorious, greatly renowned one came out again and saw the handsome Brahmanas present.
Surrounded then by Brahmanas wishing to speak blessings, he shone like the spotless moon surrounded by hosts of stars.
The son of Kunti duly honoured those twice-born, putting Dhaumya the teacher and his eldest father (Dhritarashtra) in front,
with flowers, sweets, jewels, abundant gold, cows and garments, king of kings, and various wished-for gifts.
Then a cry of "Auspicious day!" arose as if stopping heaven, holy, delighting friends and pleasing to the ear.
The voices of the twice-born, crying like swans, were heard there, of those who know the Veda, with abundant meaning, words and syllables.
Then the sound of kettledrums and of lovely conches arose, O king, as they shouted "Victory!"
When silence fell there among the Brahmana people, the Rakshasa Charvaka, disguised as a Brahmana, spoke to the king.
There, a friend of Duryodhana, in the guise of a mendicant, a Sankhya, with a topknot and triple staff, bold and fearless,
surrounded by all the Brahmanas who wished to speak blessings, more than a thousand, established in austerity and restraint, O king,
wicked, wishing harm to the great-souled Pandavas, without consulting those Brahmanas, he said to the king:

All these twice-born say, laying the word on me: 'Fie on you, a bad king, a slayer of kinsmen!'
mahabharata:12:39.27	What use is your kingdom to you, son of Kunti, having made this destruction of kinsmen and slain your teachers? Death is better than life.
Hearing the words of that dreadful Rakshasa, the twice-born were pained and cried out, overcome by his speech.
Then all those Brahmanas and King Yudhishthira were ashamed and greatly troubled and stayed silent, lord of men.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Be gracious to me, I bow and beg you; do not reproach me, a man fallen into calamity."
[Vaishampayana said:] Then, O king, all those Brahmanas said, "These words are not ours; may prosperity be yours, O king."
And the great-souled Brahmanas, learned in the Veda, purified by austerity, then knew him by the eye of knowledge.
[The Brahmanas said:] "This is Charvaka, a Rakshasa, friend of Duryodhana, in the form of a wandering mendicant, wishing his good.
We do not say so, righteous one; let such fear of yours depart; let prosperity attend you with your brothers."
[Vaishampayana said:] Then all those Brahmanas, pure, overcome with anger, with roars rebuking him, struck down the sinful Rakshasa.
He fell burned up by the energy of those expounders of Brahma, like a sprouting tree burned by Indra's thunderbolt.
Honoured, the Brahmanas went, congratulating the king, and King Pandava was glad with his friends.
[Vasudeva said:] "Brahmanas, dear one, are ever to be honoured by me in this world; they are gods walking on earth, whose speech is venom, yet who are easily pleased.
Long ago in the Krita age, dear one, a Rakshasa named Charvaka practised austerity for many years at Badari, mighty-armed one.
Offered a boon by Brahma again and again, he chose safety from all beings, Bharata.
Except for the disrespect of the twice-born, the lord of the world granted him that supreme boon, safety from all beings.
That sinner, having gained the boon, of immeasurable valour, harassed the gods, a Rakshasa of fierce deeds and great strength.
Then the gods assembled and said this to Brahma, defeated in strength, for that Rakshasa's slaying.
The imperishable god told them: 'I have arranged for that, that his death will come soon, Bharata.
A king named Duryodhana will be his friend, O king; bound by affection for him, he will disrespect Brahmanas.
There the angered Brahmanas, assailed by the insult, strong in speech, will burn that sinner, and he will go to destruction.'
This is that Rakshasa Charvaka, slain by the Brahma-rod, lying here, best of kings; do not grieve, bull of the Bharatas.
Your kinsmen are slain by kshatriya dharma, O king, and those great souls, heroes, bulls among kshatriyas, have gone to heaven."
[Gautami said:] "I have heard the words of Death and yours, serpent; but no freedom from fault has yet come to you, serpent."
[Vaishampayana said:] Thus addressed by Partha, Krishna Dvaipayana then reflected a moment and said to the king of dharma:
These two arms of mine, like iron bars, hard to approach, between which the Dhritarashtras came to ruin.
Then at Prabhasa the Yadavas lived with their wives as they pleased, as at home, with abundant food and drink.
Seeing them fallen, Pandava, the white-horsed slayer of heroes, fell, burned with grief.
As you, invincible one, come, a holy breeze blows, following your fragrance, dear one, by which we have been made happy.
